headline: Barrick: adjusted EPS up 41% on high gold prices, Mali mine back at full speed, but costs per ounce jump 24%
takeaway: Adjusted EPS rose 41% to $0.82, beating the $0.79 consensus, as revenue rose 22% to $5.07 billion. Gold output grew 6% on a like-for-like basis with the Loulo-Gounkoto mine in Mali ramping up ahead of schedule, but all-in sustaining costs rose to $1,911 an ounce. Barrick returned $1.04 billion to shareholders and the shares rose 4%.
results: Barrick Mining reported revenue of $5.07 billion for the third quarter, up 22%, and attributable adjusted EBITDA of $2.47 billion, also up 22%. Net earnings rose 1% to $1.32 billion, or $0.80 a share, while adjusted net earnings per share rose 41% to $0.82. Operating cash flow was $2.49 billion and attributable free cash flow $0.64 billion.

Gold production was 816,000 ounces, up 3% from the second quarter and 6% from a year earlier excluding divested mines, and copper production was 50,000 tonnes. Cortez in Nevada benefited from the Goldrush ramp-up, the Gold Quarry roaster at Carlin had a record quarter, and Loulo-Gounkoto produced 16% more than in the second quarter.

Costs rose sharply. Gold cost of sales was $1,950 an ounce against $1,562, total cash costs $1,386 against $1,137, and all-in sustaining costs $1,911 against $1,538, reflecting lower grades, higher royalties linked to gold prices, diesel and stronger local currencies. Barrick bought back $761 million of stock, paid a $0.175 dividend and ended with $0.9 billion of net cash.
mgmt: Chief executive Mark Hill said that a year ago management set out to earn back trust and restore Barrick’s discipline, and that this quarter marked a full year of consistent delivery, with improved safety, a stronger Nevada Gold Mines and better productivity offsetting cost pressures.

Barrick reiterated full-year guidance of 2.90 to 3.25 million ounces of gold and 190,000 to 220,000 tonnes of copper. It had already cut 2026 capital spending to $3.8–$4.2 billion, mainly because spending at the Reko Diq copper-gold project in Pakistan is under review. Year-to-date results include costs from a North American IPO project expensed in the first half and charges related to the Mali settlement.
view: Barrick spent 2025 as the gold miner that could not enjoy a gold boom: its largest African mine was seized by the Malian junta, production guidance was cut, and long-time chief executive Mark Bristow left. This report shows how much of that damage has been repaired. Loulo-Gounkoto is back under Barrick’s control and ramping faster than planned, Nevada is producing more, and adjusted earnings are up 41%. Management’s language about earning back trust is unusually candid for a mining company, and so far the numbers support it.

The cost line is the part investors should not skip. All-in sustaining costs up 24% to $1,911 an ounce mean Barrick keeps a smaller share of each dollar of gold price increase than the headline suggests. Some of the rise is mechanical — royalties rise with the gold price — but lower grades and diesel are real, and a miner whose costs climb alongside the metal price is less of a lever on gold than it appears. Barrick’s net cash and $1 billion-a-quarter shareholder returns show the margins are still wide; they are just not widening.

The strategic questions are Reko Diq and the North American listing. Reko Diq is one of the largest undeveloped copper-gold deposits in the world, but putting it under review signals concern about cost, security in Balochistan or both. The IPO project suggests Barrick may separate its Nevada and North American assets from the African and Asian ones to close the valuation discount that geopolitical risk imposes. At around 8 times trailing earnings, the market still prices Barrick as a riskier miner than Newmont or Agnico Eagle; delivering on either of these decisions could narrow that gap.
watch: Watch fourth-quarter output as North Mara reaches high-grade ore, the cost trend against 2027 guidance, the outcome of the Reko Diq review and any decision on the North American listing.
